samples.text:
The table shows how much household waste was produced in a city from 2000 to 2024, and the bar chart shows the ways that the waste was disposed.

Firstly, the total waste increased from 420 thousand tonnes in 2000 to 455 thousand tonnes in 2008. After that it decreased to 430 thousand tonnes in 2016 and 395 thousand tonnes in 2024. The waste per person had a similar pattern. It was 520 kg in 2000 and went up to 535 kg in 2008, then it fell to 480 kg and finally 425 kg in 2024.

In the bar chart, landfill was the main method in 2000 with 79%, but it decreased a lot and in 2024 it was only 12%. On the other hand, recycling and composting increase from 14% to 30% in 2008, 45% in 2016 and 52% in 2024. Incineration also went up from 7% in 2000 to 36% in 2024, although it only rise slightly between 2000 and 2008.

Overall, the city produced less waste at the end of the period, and less waste goes to landfill while more waste was recycled or burned.
samples.why: Overview present but general and placed last · both visuals covered accurately · mechanical linking (Firstly, After that, On the other hand) · repetitive vocabulary · errors in verb forms, tense and a comma splice.

samples.text:
The table gives information about the quantity of household waste produced in a city between 2000 and 2024, while the bar chart shows the proportions of this waste that were landfilled, recycled or composted, and incinerated.

Overall, the amount of waste rose slightly at first but then fell, ending below its 2000 level. At the same time, there was a dramatic shift away from landfill towards recycling and incineration.

Total household waste stood at 420 thousand tonnes in 2000 and peaked at 455 thousand tonnes in 2008. It then declined to 430 thousand tonnes in 2016 and to 395 thousand tonnes in 2024. The amount of waste per person followed a similar trend, increasing from 520 kg to 535 kg before dropping steadily to 425 kg by 2024.

As for disposal, landfill accounted for 79% of waste in 2000, but its share decreased continuously to just 12% in 2024. In contrast, recycling and composting grew rapidly from 14% to 52%, becoming the main method from 2016 onwards. Incineration for energy was the least used method at first, at only 7% in 2000, but it rise to 21% in 2016 and 36% by 2024, which meant it overtook landfill at some point after 2016.
samples.why: Clear overview of both the waste trend and the change in disposal · key features logically organised · good range of linkers · some less common vocabulary (landfilled, overtook) · one minor verb error.

samples.text:
The table presents the total and per capita amounts of household waste generated in a city in four years between 2000 and 2024, and the bar chart shows how this waste was dealt with.

The volume of waste peaked in 2008 and declined thereafter, while methods of disposal were transformed: landfill, initially the overwhelmingly dominant method, became the least used, overtaken by both recycling and incineration.

The city produced 420 thousand tonnes of household waste in 2000, rising to 455 thousand tonnes in 2008. Output then fell in each subsequent year shown, reaching 395 thousand tonnes in 2024. Waste per person mirrored this trend but fell more steeply, from a high of 535 kg in 2008 to 425 kg in 2024, roughly a fifth lower.

In 2000, almost four fifths of household waste (79%) was sent to landfill, with recycling and composting handling 14% and incineration just 7%. Over the following 24 years, landfill's share shrank to a mere 12%, whereas recycling and composting nearly quadrupled to 52%, making it the leading method by 2016. Incineration for energy, which had grown only marginally by 2008, expanded rapidly thereafter, accounting for over a third of waste (36%) by 2024.
samples.why: Incisive overview capturing the reversal in disposal methods · accurate figures and derived comparisons chosen selectively · cohesion managed skilfully · precise vocabulary (per capita, mirrored, shrank) · wide range of error-free structures.
